newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Latest crew-imposed Mir crisis may be resolved.
newsitem.headline: Latest crew-imposed Mir crisis may be resolved.

text.p: Russia's crippled Mir space station was caught up in a new crisis on Thursday when a cosmonaut mistakenly unplugged a vital computer cable and plunged the craft into darkness, but officials said the mission would go ahead.

"We are not planning to return the crew, we are planning to continue the flight," mission director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters after a tense day at Mission Control outside Moscow. "The crew are now being sent to sleep, they are tired."

He said Mir's orientation towards the sun would be restored on Friday morning and the gyrodines system which keeps the station in the best position to accumulate solar energy would be restored on Saturday.
Another improvement came when Earth and the Russian-U.S. crew restored a vital computer link which would allow experts to analyse data and help the cosmonauts repair the craft.

"We have received telemetry of a good quality and we are recording it now," said one of the experts as the screens of the computers, dead since the station lost most of its energy early in the day, came alive.
Thursday's crisis was the worst since a collision with an unmanned cargo craft on June 25 which pierced the Spekrt module and cut off up to half of Mir's energy.

The three-man crew, whose commander developed a probably stress-induced heart problem this week, had to sit in their Soyuz escape capsule to communicate with Earth by radio on Thursday and were using flashlights to get around the darkened station.
"I should stress it is an especially unpleasant situation. It very much recalls the situation we were in after the crash," Solovyov told reporters on Thursday morning.

The crew have canned oxygen that will last for just five days, while the temperature and humidity will remain bearable for two or three days without power. That set a clear time limit on re-starting Mir's life-support machines, including the oxygen generators.

Without the gyroscopes, the crew had to fire rocket engines on the Soyuz craft -- thereby running down the fuel they have to spare to get home if things go wrong. But a spokesman said escape capsule was burning little fuel and had plenty left.
Frantic efforts by the crew and the Mission Control appeared to bear fruit by the end of the day.
Mission doctor Igor Goncharov told Reuters the crew had succeeded in accumulating sufficient solar power in Mir's batteries to eventually re-start the gyroscopic guidance system.
This accumulated energy appeared to allow the crew re-establish the computer link. The link-up ended with a "Go to sleep, good luck" message from Earth.
"I expect the ship will be re-oriented by tomorrow morning, by about nine a.m. (0500 GMT)," Solovyov said.
But Solovyov said the latest crisis probably meant that the repair works in the Spektr module would have to be put off once more. He said the date for the work would be decided later.

The sortie to the Spektr has already been put off after commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, developed an irregular heartbeat. NASA physicist Michael Foale, 40, is now due to step in to a spacesuit to help engineer Alexander Lazutkin, 39.

The tension was palpable at Mission Control in the biggest drama since last month's collision -- also possibly caused by a crew error -- which cut power by up to half and nearly cost the men their lives when one of Mir's modules was holed.
"This is a kindergarten!" a frustrated Solovyov said aloud after telling the crew repeatedly to shut down systems.

"This was purely human error," he said of the latest crisis. Officials have neither confirmed nor denied reports that a basic mistake by Tsibliyev caused the June 25 collision nor an Russian news agency report that it was he who made Thursday's error.

Officials said the job may now be left for a Russian-French crew due to arrive on Mir on August 7 -- if Mir is still habitable. If the present crew abandoned ship, Mir would die as its systems cannot operate without human hands on the controls.

The original collision was the worst accident in its 11 years in space but by no means an isolated mishap, and had already raised questions over whether it should be ditched before a new international space station is launched next year.
Russian officials, whose agency depends on the foreign cash Mir brings in to keep much of the post-Soviet space industry aloft, insist they do not want to abandon the station.
